bullets.text: In and out in minutes, not rushed

sections.name: What Section
sections.title: Someone told you it's a disc

paras.t: Maybe an MRI said herniated. Maybe another doctor said bulging. Maybe a friend said slipped. Or maybe nobody has told you anything yet, but you've got back pain that won't settle and pain running into a leg.
Whichever word you've heard, you're in the right place.

sections.name: What Section
sections.title: Bulging, herniated, slipped: what the words mean

paras.t: Your discs are the cushions between the bones of your spine.
Bulging means the disc is pushing out past where it should sit, a bit like a tire that's low on air.
Herniated means the soft inner part has pushed through the tougher outer layer.
Slipped is the everyday name for both. Discs don't actually slip.
Any of them can press on a nerve, which is why disc problems so often come with sciatica, numbness, or tingling down a leg.

callouts.title: What X-rays show and what they don't.
callouts.text: Discs are soft tissue, so they don't show up on an X-ray. What does show up is the space between the bones. When that space is thinning, it tells Dr. Morgan the disc is wearing down. In the lower back, that disc-space thinning is the change he sees most. If he needs to see the disc itself, that's what an MRI is for.

sections.title: Find it, fix it, keep it from coming back

paras.t: When we'd send you for an MRI. If you haven't improved after about six weeks, or you finish a plan with less change than expected, Dr. Morgan will refer you for one.

bullets.body: A full history and exam, digital X-rays on site when the exam calls for them, and an MRI referral when it's needed.

Adjustments plus spinal decompression. Decompression is a slow, controlled stretch that takes pressure off the disc and the nerve it's pressing on. Dr. Morgan never does decompression on its own. The adjustment is always part of it.
Disc problems in the lower back are usually chronic. The goal is a new baseline: get you out of pain, then slow the wear down from there with maintenance, about once every two weeks.

sections.name: First Visit Section
sections.title: Your first visit, start to finish

paras.t: First visit runs about 30 minutes. After that, most visits take a few minutes. Dr. Morgan built the practice around working people.

steps.title: We find out what is actually happening
steps.text: Full history and exam. What hurts, what you have already tried, what you want to get back to doing. Any necessary digital X-rays, taken on site.

steps.title: Dr. Morgan shows you the imaging, same day
steps.text: He marks it up and walks you through it right there. You will see what he sees. Most patients get their first adjustment the same visit.

steps.title: You come back for the full report
steps.text: Within a few days, Dr. Morgan lays out what he found and exactly what he recommends. What it will take, how long, and what it costs. Then you decide.

sections.name: What Section
sections.title: How long until this actually feels better

paras.t: Most people want a number before they start. Dr. Morgan will give you one, just not before he has examined you and looked at your imaging. He will not guess.
What he can tell you up front is how it usually goes, including the part most offices skip: the first two weeks are uneven.
If you are only trying to get out of pain, a shorter plan can do that. If you want it to stay fixed, it takes about 90 days. Dr. Morgan will give you both options and let you pick.

tags.text: Inconsistent, and that's normal. You'll have a good day and think it's fixed, then a bad one and think it's not working. Dr. Morgan warns you about this on day one. Real change usually starts around the end of week two, and better sleep is often the first thing people notice.

The bulk of the plan. A typical plan is about 24 visits over 90 days, two to three times a week at the start, then less often as you improve. Some people need fewer. Dr. Morgan checks your progress along the way.
Most patients move to maintenance, about once every two weeks. Some stop entirely. Dr. Morgan will tell you when you're there.

faqs.q: What's the difference between herniated and bulging?
faqs.a: A bulging disc pushes out past where it should sit. A herniated disc has its soft inner part pushing through the outer layer. Both can press on a nerve, and both are treated the same way here.
Most disc problems don't need surgery. Dr. Morgan will tell you if your exam or imaging points to a surgeon, and if it does, he'll say so.

faqs.q: Can you see a herniated disc on an X-ray?
faqs.a: Not directly. X-rays show the space between the bones, and a thinning space tells Dr. Morgan the disc is wearing down. An MRI shows the disc itself, and he'll refer you for one if it's needed.
Often, with disc problems. Dr. Morgan recommends it when your exam and imaging support it. It's a cash service, $75 per session, and it always goes alongside your adjustments.
Not to start. Dr. Morgan refers for one if you haven't improved after about six weeks, or if a plan ends with less change than expected.

faqs.q: Will the adjustment hurt with a disc problem?
faqs.a: Dr. Morgan starts gentle on the first visit to get a feel for your spine. If something is tender, tell him and he works around it.
